events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9��Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ��———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Decision Making with AI: Think Better, Choose Smarter (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) We are rapidly heading into an AI-driven future. At first, we feared it might cost us jobs, but now we see the bigger risk: it could cost us our judgment. When we outsource our thinking to fast answers, we lose the ability to ask better questions. To be ready for this future — to truly empower it — we must strengthen our uniquely human potential: clarity, critical thinking, and decision-making. That's what this workshop is about. In this interactive, hands-on session, participants will learn how to frame better decisions — before they ever open a chatbot. Using a practical tool called the Decision Framing Canvas, they'll work through a real business case and discover how to define decisions as real, actionable choices (not just goals or problems). At every step, participants will collaborate with AI — not to skip the thinking, but to deepen it. They'll use AI to challenge assumptions, expand options, and uncover what might be missing. This workshop helps participants take back control of their thinking in an AI-saturated world. It's not about better prompts — it's about better minds. Participants will walk away with a repeatable method to make smarter, clearer decisions in their daily work — and a deeper understanding of how to use AI not just as a tool, but as a thinking partner. No technical background required. Just bring your brain, your curiosity, and your favorite LLM (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc).Learning Outcomes: –Use the Decision Framing Canvas to define complex decisions as actionable choices between real options clearly. –Collaborate with AI to challenge assumptions, uncover blind spots, and expand decision options before jumping to solutions. –Learn key principles for working effectively with AI as a thinking partner — and apply them immediately to real decision-making scenarios.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Student Hosted Symposium in Organic Chemistry
events.description: Dave MacMillan, A. Barton Hepburn Professor of Chemistry, Princeton UniversityThe Development of Photocatalytic Reactions of Value to Chemists and BiologistsThis lecture will discuss the application of visible light photocatalysis to the discovery or invention of transformations that will be conceptually or synthetically valuable (and sometimes, hopefully, both). We will describe why a healthy balance of reaction discovery and mechanistic understanding has been important to the development of a field of research that is now being widely adopted in medicinal chemistry settings. In particular, we will discuss the application of photocatalysis to the development of new metallaphotoredox coupling reactions involving SH2 mechanisms, a development that we hope will have an impact on the discovery of new biologically relevant molecules. Finally, we will examine an exciting recent application of photoredox catalysis in my group; namely, the high-resolution µ-map technology, which provides a powerful means to probe biological pathways at the subcellular level.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Failure by design: The California energy crisis and the limits of market planning
events.description: With Georg Rilinger, Assistant Professor of Technological Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Strategic Management, MIT Sloan School of Management The Western U.S. energy crisis was one of the great financial disasters of the past century. The crisis began in April 2000, when price spikes started to rattle California's electricity markets. Decades later, some blame economic fundamentals and ignorant politicians, while others accuse the energy sellers who raided the markets. In Failure by Design, sociologist Georg Rilinger offers a different explanation, one that focuses on the practical challenges of market design. The unique physical attributes of electricity made it exceedingly difficult to introduce markets into the coordination of the electricity system, so market designers were brought in to construct the infrastructures that coordinate how market participants interact. An exercise in social engineering, these infrastructures were intended to guide market actors toward behavior that would produce optimal market results and facilitate grid management. Yet, though these experts spent their days worrying about incentive misalignment and market manipulation, they unintentionally created a system riddled with opportunities for destructive behavior. Join us at BESI for this talk as Rilinger illuminates the California energy crisis and develops a broader theoretical framework for thinking about markets as the products of organizational planning and the limits of social engineering.Register Now (https://forms.gle/NGwAc9WuQseojhox9) About the speaker Georg Rilinger is an assistant professor of economic and organization sociology at MIT Sloan School of Management, where he holds the Fred Kayne Career Development Professorship. His research examines organizational, cultural, and political reasons why technocratic expertise — from Nobel Prize-winning market designers to financial regulators — so often fails to prevent market failures, drawing on archival research, interviews, and ethnographic methods. He is the author of Failure by Design: The California Energy Crisis and the Limits of Market Planning (University of Chicago Press, 2024), which won the Viviana Zelizer Prize for Best Book in Economic Sociology. His work has appeared in the American Journal of Sociology, Socio-Economic Review, Theory and Society, and others.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Local Housing Market Experiences and Homeownership Decisions"
events.description: Abstract:An extensive literature documents that personally experienced returns disproportionately shape households' expectations and financial decisions. Whether these experiences lead households to make costly financial mistakes is less understood. Using residence histories from the University of California Consumer Credit Panel, we construct person-specific housing market experiences from county-level nominal house-price returns since age 18. A 1 percentage point increase in experienced returns raises the quarterly probability of entry into homeownership by 8.4% relative to the baseline mean. Higher experienced returns also predict greater mortgage borrowing and subsequent distress: among new homeowners, a 1 percentage point increase raises the probability of mortgage delinquency within four years of purchase by 2.3 percentage points. Under rational expectations, experienced returns should not predict delinquency conditional on borrower and market characteristics. Experience-based extrapolation can raise mortgage payments relative to available cash, increasing the likelihood of delinquency.

events.title: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America
events.description: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America Thursday, October 6, 12:30 - 2 pm Lunchtime Talk Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/yD8LTQaNvyDeTDCa6)How to Survive Authoritarianism (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324098799) offers Americans the tools needed to face the threat of authoritarianism today—from a country that's been surviving it for a century. Across the globe, far-right extremists are gaining power as checks and balances between branches of government dissolve at alarming rates. Author and activist Maria Kuznetsova and researcher Dan Storyev - who grew up in 2000s Russia when Vladimir Putin was tightening his grasp on the country and suffocating civic life - share the language that allowed them to talk about authoritarianism and to subvert it. Friends of Kuznetsova and Storyev's began asking what life was like in Russia, most having never experienced a dictatorship but increasingly worried they were about to learn. In attempting to answer their friends' questions of "How do you overcome fear of the state?" and maybe the most harrowing, "When is it too late?," Kuznetsova and Storyev draw upon their own experiences and the broader cultural memory of Russia to explore the basics of how authoritarian structures are built, and how ordinary people can resist. How to Survive Authoritarianism offers one hundred Russian idioms and turns of phrase for this purpose, from "apparatchik" to "samizdat." Some, like "power vertical," coined by Putin, give name to a hyper-centralized form of government with a top-down hierarchy of power. Others are more playful, like mnogohodovochka ("master plan"), used to deride bizarre, misguided state measures. Taken together, they make up the vocabulary we need to understand what is really taking place in our current moment and offer a roadmap to what might still lie ahead. In Russia, the dual reality of the truth, and what is called the truth by the government, has been the law of the land for generations. Over the years, a vernacular of double-speak emerged, one that helped everyday people make sense of how illiberalism makes itself known in daily life.

events.title: Seminar 221, Industrial Organization: Ming-yen Ho "Picking Winners or Building Them? Central and Local Government Venture Capital in Chinese Semiconductors"
events.description: JMC PracticeAbstract: Does the level of government matter for industrial policy? I compare firms invested by local government, central government, and private venture capital (VC) funds in China's semiconductor industry. Central and private VCs invest in the nation's most productive firms, while local VCs back smaller, less productive local champions, suggesting misallocation for the national government maximizing industry sales. Yet event studies suggest that local government-backed firms experience larger post-investment gains of about 27% in revenue productivity relative to not yet invested firms, while private- and central government- backed firms see no detectable change. As local government VCs hold a smaller portfolio and are sit closer to their portfolio firms, they participate more in management by adding directors with graduate degrees and foreign education. Board changes account for 42% of the central-local productivity effect gap. In a model combining VC selection, firm productivity and capital responses, and import competition, the sales of domestic semiconductor firms in 2023 would have been 12% lower had private VCs allocate government VCs' deals, and 4% lower if the central government allocates local governments' investments. Dynamic productivity growth from local VC investments outweighs the selection of central and private VCs on initially larger and more efficient firms.

events.description: Personal AI agents like Meta's recently launched Muse could change the way how consumers interact with digital services and have a transformational impact on the functioning of digital markets. Against this background, the talk explores how the shift towards agentic commerce challenges several core concepts and regulatory tools of a human-centric consumer law – from mandatory disclosures and design-based consumer law standards to rules against unfair commercial practices – and how consumer law must adapt to work for humans… and machines. events.title: Lily Beckett | Poems on the London Underground (and Beyond)
events.description: Since 1986, Poems in the Underground has enabled commuters on London to randomly encounter poetry – classic and contemporary, British and international – while traveling on the tube, via poster cards slotted in the carriage advertising spaces. In conversation with Professor Eric Falci, Lily Beckett's talk will explore the history, development, and impact of Poems on the Underground as a public poetry project. Founded by Judith Chaiken (a native New Yorker), the idea for the project arose in the middle of Thatcher's premiership, a political moment characterised by an ideological turn away from the public and towards the private. Since its founding, the project has continued, uninterrupted, for 40 years, and has inspired multiple spin-off schemes abroad, with poetry being installed on transit systems in cities like Dublin, Paris, and New York. Adopting a socio-poetic angle, this talk offers Poems on the Underground as a prompt for further considering the value of poetry in public spaces. What does poetry do for the 'travelling public' of modern cities – whether in the 1980s in Britain under Thatcher, or today, anywhere in the world, in the age of AI?Lily Beckett is undertaking a PhD in Comparative Literatures and Cultures at the University of Bristol. She is currently a visiting scholar at UC Berkeley's Institute of European Studies. Her thesis investigates the connections between intermedial poetics and radical politics in the latter decades of the 20th century, across a range of global contexts. Before Bristol, she completed her master's degree in Comparative Literature at King's College London, and her undergraduate studies in Classics and English at Oxford University. She recently appeared on Soho Radio to discuss the lasting relevance of the 18th century poet William Blake, and her research papers can be found (or are forthcoming) in the academic journals Interfaces and Women's Studies.Eric Falci is a professor in the Department of English. He is the author of three books: Continuity and Change in Irish Poetry, 1966-2010 (2012); The Cambridge Introduction to British Poetry, 1945-2010 (2015); and The Value of Poetry (2020), as well as a number of essays on Irish and British poetry. With Paige Reynolds, he co-edited Irish Literature in Transition, 1980-2020 (2022). He is the series editor of Cambridge Elements in Poetry and Poetics, and the editor of the Cambridge History of Irish Poetry, scheduled to be published in 2026. He is also the author of a book of poetry, Late Along the Edgelands (2019). His research focus concerns the problem of form in twentieth and twenty-first century poetry. He teaches classes on modern Irish and British literature, and poetry.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Kevin Wilson, Deputy Director of the Chemical Sciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National LaboratoryChemical Kinetics in MicrocompartmentsOver the last 10+ years there has emerged some evidence that when a reaction vessel is reduced to the micron-sized dimensions (e.g. droplets), photochemical and bimolecular reactions speed up by many orders of magnitude. The mechanism(s) for rate acceleration in droplets remains unclear but has potential implications for understanding the chemistry of the atmosphere where cloud droplets and aerosols play important roles. A key uncertainty in the interpretation of droplet kinetics is how to properly link reaction rates measured in beaker scale containers with those occurring in micron-sized spaces. This challenge lies, in large part, in understanding the complex kinetic coupling of adsorption, desorption, and diffusion that link chemistry occurring at the surface of an aerosol or droplet with processes occurring in its interior. In this talk I will review our work combining novel single droplet and microfluidics experiments with stochastic reaction diffusion models to develop a robust understanding of reaction rates and processes in small compartments where interfaces play a prominent role.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "A Macroeconomic Model of the Cross-Section of Currencies"
events.description: Abstract: We study the cross-section of currencies using a macroeconomic model with heterogeneous countries, segmented asset markets, and risk-averse financial intermediaries. The model admits a two-factor structure of bilateral exchange rates. The factors combine global business cycle shocks and financial shocks that reprice the business cycle risk. Countries' exposures to these factors are heterogeneous and depend on their reliance on commodity exports and dollar asset holdings. We estimate the resulting factor structure empirically and use it to quantify the model. Our results indicate substantial heterogeneity in the drivers of dollar exchange rates across countries. Economies with high commodity exposure or low dollar holdings are risky, and their exchange rates fluctuate in response to global output and risk shocks. The exchange rates of countries with low commodity incidence and high dollar assets are less volatile, and their fluctuations are mostly determined by idiosyncratic local shocks.

events.title: Commutative Algebra and Algebraic Geometry Seminar: Chow Vanishing and Motives of Cluster Varieties
events.description: Speaker: Josephine Hlavinka, UC BerkeleyProgress over the last decade has shown that the cohomologies of full rank, locally acyclic cluster varieties enjoy remarkable combinatorial structures. Crucial in this program has been the observation that these cohomology groups are, in certain Hodge theoretic senses, about as simple as possible. In this talk we will discuss a motivic lift of this observation. In particular we establish that the Voevodsky motives of really full rank sink-recurrent cluster varieties are mixed Tate and split over Q (strengthening results of Lam and Speyer), and we prove that their integral Chow groups are all trivial.

events.title: Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive
events.description: n her new book, Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive, Na'ama Rokem investigates written exchanges by a range of literary twentieth century authors, including Hannah Arendt, Gershom Scholem, Yehuda Amichai, Ludwig Strauss, Erich Auerbach, Walter Benjamin, Leah Goldberg, Peter Szondi, Paul Celan, and Tuvia Ruebner. This remarkable bilingual archive encompasses not only letters but also drafts, reviews, and other ephemeral documents. Written in German and Hebrew, these documents were sent to and from Jerusalem, primarily in the decades following 1948. The writers at the center of Rokem's study contend with the genocidal violence that brought the rich historical relation between German and Hebrew to a seeming end. They also grapple, in different ways, with the new reality in Israel/Palestine in the wake of the founding of the State of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba. The bilingual conversation that crosses over between German and Hebrew in these letters thus centers around the question of Jewish fate in the twentieth century and is immersed in negotiations about Jewish nationalism, the Zionist movement, and the possibilities of Jewish poetry. In the space between German and Hebrew, Rokem argues, the protagonists of her study articulate forms of ambivalence and doubt that remain absent from their published writings. In this book presentation, Rokem will discuss forms of belonging and resistance that emerged in relation to the Zionist movement throughout the twentieth century, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of Jewish nationalism and its discontents.To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/5p6thMQDtfz5LarP8)Na'ama Rokem teaches Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of Chicago, where she has served as director of the Joyce Z. and Jacob Greenberg Center for Jewish Studies and as chair of the Department of Comparative Literature. Zionism in Translation: Encounters in the German-Hebrew Archive (University of Chicago Press, 2026) is her second book. Her first book, Prosaic Conditions: Heinrich Heine and the Spaces of Zionist Literature, was published by Northwestern University Press in 2013. It uses the case of the reception and translation of the works of German-Jewish poet Heinrich Heine to argue that prose - as a figure of thought, a mode and a medium - played an instrumental role in the literary foundations of the Zionist revolution. Currently, she is working as one of the co-editors of the forthcoming Volume IV.2 of the Critical Edition of the Complete Works of Hannah Arendt (https://hannah-arendt-edition.net/index.html?lang=en) (Essays and Short Writings on Jewish Politics) and starting a new research project on Zionism and pedagogy. Rokem has been involved in a number of collaborative projects, including The Quest for Modern Language: Between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/the-quest-for-modern-language-between-the-mediterranean-and-black-sea-1820-1948#:~:text=This%20is%20a%20collaborative%2C%20multidisciplinary,19th%20and%20early%2020th%20centuries.), and Translation Networks and the Stakes of Comparison: Convergences and Crossings Between Arabic and Hebrew (https://neubauercollegium.uchicago.edu/research/translation-networks), both sponsored by the Neubauer Collegium on Culture and Society at the University of Chicago, and the Oak Woods Cemetery (https://www.oakwoodsproject.org/) project, a public history initiative that uses a historic cemetery in Woodlawn as a site for teaching, programming, and researching the history of the South Side of Chicago, with a particular interest in the complexly intertwined histories of African Americans and Jews in the city. This project has received funding from the NEH, the Mellon Foundation, and the Women's Board at the University of Chicago. ��� If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible. events.description: UC Berkeley School of Public Health Dean's Speaker Series: Lynn Barr on Reimagining Public Health October 6, 2026 5:30-7:00 p.m. Followed by reception 7:00–8:00 p.m. *or online via Zoom 2121 Berkeley Way, Colloquia Room 1104 (BWW 1st Floor) Featuring Caravan Health and Rural Health Innovation Program Founder Lynn Barr, (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/articles/spotlight/alumni/a-transformational-legacy-for-public-health) MPH '11With an introduction from Dean Michael C. Lu. Health care innovator Lynn Barr has been at the forefront of a movement to reimagine healthcare for rural communities across the United States. After founding Caravan Health to help small, rural health care providers team up to manage patient care and the Medicare system, Barr was appointed to the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, which advises Congress Medicare policy in 2022. Appalled by the low vaccination rates and corresponding high death rates from COVID-19, she founded UC Berkeley's Rural Health Innovation Program in 2023, which educates and mentors public health professionals from rural communities to empower them to drive changes in both policy and practice, providing 100 full-ride MPH scholarships to date in 30 states. Barr has led programs that have improved care for more than one million Medicare patients, and she's not done yet. At this special Dean's Speaker event, Barr will talk with Kimberly MacPherson (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/kimberly-macpherson), faculty director for the Rural Health Innovation Program and MPH/MBA Program at UC Berkeley School of Public Health, about the lessons she's learned throughout her esteemed career on how and why to influence policy for the better health of all. events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Modeling Tumor Immunosurveillance
events.description: Abstract: While cancer immunotherapy has provided unprecedented clinical outcomes in certain settings, only a subset of patients benefit. We are exploring the hypothesis that changes in physical properties, in particular viscoelasticity, of solid tumors alters immune cell phenotype and function. Using biomaterials that allow independent control over key variables, we find that the rate of matrix stress relaxation has dramatic effects on immune cells, including antigen presenting and T cells, and controls cell-cell interactions mediating immune cell responses.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Zachary B. Dozier (Stanford University School of Medicine)
events.description: Hear from a leading expert in the field! Join us on Wednesday, October 7th for a seminar with Zachary B. Dozier (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/zach-b-dozier-phd), Assistant Professor of Pediatrics (Clinical Informatics) and of Medicine (Computational Medicine) at Stanford University School of Medicine. Dr. Dozier will present "Targeted Learning: Causal Inference in Long COVID and Pediatrics." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.Abstract: I will discuss machine learning applications for causal inference in large electronic health record (EHR) databases. First, I will describe our recently completed work evaluating preventive interventions for Long COVID through target trial emulation in the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative (N3C), where we assessed IL-6 receptor antagonists, diabetes treatments (metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists), and SSRIs. I will then discuss new and ongoing projects applying this approach to pediatric health in Epic Cosmos, an EHR database of more than 300 million patients across the US. Finally, I will discuss career planning and the faculty job search process.Bio: Zach B. Dozier (formerly Butzin-Dozier) is an Assistant Professor at the Stanford University School of Medicine in the Department of Pediatrics, Division of Clinical Informatics, with a joint appointment in the Department of Medicine, Division of Computational Medicine. His research applies machine learning and artificial intelligence for causal inference via electronic health record data. He draws from large-scale databases, such as Epic Cosmos, PEDSnet, and the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative, to answer pressing questions in pediatric and infectious disease medicine. His research evaluates vaccine effectiveness, drug repurposing, and the long-term sequelae of viral infection, including Long COVID. He aims to bridge rigorous biostatistical methodology with clinically meaningful research questions. He received his PhD in Epidemiology and MPH from UC Berkeley, and he is an NIAID K01 recipient.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Leonardo Martinez: "Tuberculosis Risk During Pregnancy and Postpartum Among Women With HIV in Kenya"
events.description: Leo Martinez is an assistant professor in the Division of Epidemiology at the UC Berkeley School of Public Health. He studies the epidemiology of tuberculosis and other infectious diseases, with a focus on how social, biological, and programmatic factors shape who becomes infected, who develops disease, and who experiences long-term health consequences. Dr. Martinez uses epidemiologic, statistical, and quantitative approaches to study tuberculosis transmission and prevention in high-burden settings and among populations at elevated risk, including children, people living with HIV, people with diabetes, and incarcerated populations. Much of his work centers on early-life risk factors for pediatric tuberculosis, the role of nutrition and growth in tuberculosis risk, tuberculosis transmission in congregate settings, and the relationship between tuberculosis and chronic disease outcomes. His research is highly collaborative and is conducted with colleagues and public health partners in the United States and globally, including in South Africa, Kenya, Brazil, China, and Indonesia. Through these partnerships, his work aims to produce evidence that can inform tuberculosis prevention policy, improve screening and treatment strategies, and reduce disparities in tuberculosis burden. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Dr. Martinez was a faculty member in the Department of Epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health.

events.title: Nina Miolane: Science of Intelligence Seminar Series
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: The Loft Hour: Mark Minch-de Leon + Latanya d. Tigner
events.description: Elevate your lunch break with The Loft Hour, a year-long series that invites Berkeley Arts faculty to riff on their work over lunch, in an informal conversation moderated by an ARC-affiliated faculty member. The year will kick off in October with welcoming Mark Minch-de Leon (Associate Professor, Film & Media) and Latanya d. Tigner (Assistant Professor, Dance) in conversation with Tadiwa Madenga (Assistant Professor, English). Mark Minch-de Leon is an Associate Professor in the Department of Film & Media. He was most recently an Associate Professor of Indigenous studies in the Department of English at UC Riverside where he also directed the California Center for Native Nations. His current research focuses on Indigenous anticolonial resistance and its relation to communism and anarchism, radical conceptions of community and understandings of violence, and Indigenous theories and practices of aesthetics and media-making before, beyond, against, and after settler life. His recently published book, Indigenous Inhumanities: California Indian Studies After the Apocalypse looks at the anticolonial, nonvitalist dimensions of California Indian intellectual and cultural resurgence in the wake of destruction. His publications include Race and the Limitations of 'the Human' in After the Human, and Atlas for a Destroyed World: Frank Day's Painting as Work of Nonvital Revitalization in Native American and Indigenous Studies. Professor Minch-de Leon received his AA in Liberal Studies from Butte Community College, his BA in Philosophy from CSU Chico, and his PhD in Rhetoric with an Emphasis in Gender, Women, and Sexuality from UC Berkeley. He is a member of the Susanville Indian Rancheria and co-founder of the California Indian Studies and Scholars Association. Latanya d. Tigner, a longtime member and administrator of Oakland's esteemed Dimensions Dance Theater, Inc., holds a B.A. in Physical Education/Dance, a Master's in Arts Administration, and is certified in the Yanvalu Level 2 of Talawa Technique™, the first American to do so. Her time with Dimensions includes studying Guinea, Senegalese, South African, Cuban, Haitian, modern, and jazz dance, as well as performing multidisciplinary contemporary works anchored in African diasporic dance and the African American experience. Latanya's research-based choreographic work has afforded her the opportunity to serve as co-artistic director of the renowned San Francisco Ethnic Dance Festival from 2018-2021, as well as led to the creation of Dancing Cy(i)phers in 2019. Latanya became a lecturer for TDPS in 2016 after leading the dance program at Contra Costa College for eight years. In 2018, she developed the course African Dance Presence in Hip Hop, based on her Here We Go Again workshop developed in 2014 that unfolds her research and "movement line" pedagogy. In Spring 2021, she received The Michael Mansfield and Randy Sweringen Social Justice Award for Artistic Excellence in Creating a More Equitable and Inclusive World. Latanya has commissioned works for Dimensions Dance Theater, Black Choreographers Festival, Robert Moses' Kin, UC Berkeley, Mills College, and has presented work in SF Ethnic Dance Festival, CubaCaribe, and Mabina Dance Festival (Congo-Brazzaville). She has also choreographed for SF Shakespeare, Oakland Theater Project, Lorraine Hansberry Theater, Cal Shakes, Contra Costa College, Li Smith's Victorious, and co-choreographed Delina Brooks' An Open Love Letter to Black Fathers. She received best choreography nominations in theater in 2017 and 2025. Her new work, Reclaiming the Void, will premiere in collaboration with the creator of the Talawa Technique, Dr. Thomas Talawa Presto. She has presented workshops at Collegium of the African Diaspora Dance (CADD), International Association of Black in Dance (IABD), California Dance Education Association (CDEA), National Dance Education Organization (NDEO), Intangible Roots at USC, Show and Prove at UC Riverside, University of the West Indies (Barbados), and in Paris. She has also served as a member of the Hewlett Foundation's Arts Education Task Force, a board member for the California Dance Education Association, and as an advisor for Alliance for California Traditional Arts' Taproot Initiative. Latanya currently serves on the board of directors for the Alliance for California Traditional Arts. Tadiwa Madenga is a scholar of African and Black diasporic literature, gender and sexuality, and print cultures. Her research is concerned with the relationship between literature and sexuality which she traces through 20th and 21st century African book fairs and their subgenres: keynotes, book stalls, magazines, poetry. Across her academic and creative projects, her reading practice centers archival work and site specificity as critical methods for literary analysis. These interests converge in her current research project which focuses on the emergence of African queer literature and politics through the Zimbabwe International Book Fair. The book fair was a preeminent destination for African literature and arts throughout the 1980s and 1990s, but it also became notorious for staging public debates around race and homosexuality. By examining how the book fair functioned as a contested site that codified the limits and possibilities of sexual freedom, the project also reconsiders what genres and spaces are imagined to be the foundational subjects of African literary studies and Black queer studies. Madenga's research has been supported by various fellowships and grants at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs, the Center for Black, Brown, and Queer Studies, and the Hutchins Centre for African and African American Research at Harvard University.

events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) About: Baskets were among the most versatile tools of the Jomon period in Japan. People used them to gather, process, store, and carry food and other materials. Because baskets rarely survive in archaeological contexts, they have long been on the margins of Jomon archaeology. Over the past four decades, however, waterlogged sites have produced well-preserved basketry. Advances in plant-material identification have also changed what these objects can tell us. For my dissertation, which draws on excavations at the Higashimyo site in Saga, Japan, I explore how basketry shaped, and was shaped by, Jomon people's long-term relationships with their plant environments. Baskets are direct material evidence of plant management. They show which raw materials people chose, when they harvested them, and what they knew about preparing fibers such as vines, bamboo, and woody shoots. Whether Jomon people deliberately tended plant stands is still debated, but basketry offers important clues.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: The Dry Ten Martini Problem
events.description: Speaker: Dan Borgnia, UC BerkeleyAbstract: We prove persistence of every almost Mathieu gap up to critical coupling by showing that its maximum logarithmic height is nondecreasing in the coupling λ. This allows us to propagate gap opening from perturbative seed gaps at small coupling to the critical point $\lambda =1$, resolving the Dry Ten Martini Problem. Maximum height-type arguments have been previously introduced in the quasiperiodic operator literature, but the non-decreasing property required restoring time-reversal symmetry to the problem. To this end, we studied the time-reversal-symmetric combination $h_+=1/2(h+\bar h)$ of the almost Mathieu operator $h$ with its magnetic inverse $\barh $ and expressed the height derivative as a magnetic-sector charge, whose conservation yielded the required monotonicity.

events.title: Probability Seminar: Tatiana Smirnova-Nagnibeda "Limits of graphs and invariant measures"
events.description: Abstract: Benjamini–Schramm convergence describes local limits of sequences of finite graphs viewed from uniformly chosen roots, giving rise to unimodular random rooted graphs. In this talk, we will discuss these limits for Rauzy graphs—sequences of finite graphs naturally associated with symbolic dynamical systems—in cases of both subexponential and exponential word complexity. We will see that Benjamini-Schramm limits of Rauzy graphs provide concrete graphical realizations of shift-invariant measures, including the measure of maximal entropy for primitive subshifts of finite type.

events.title: Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control
events.description: Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control Wednesday, October 7, 3:30 to 5 pm Institute of International Studies, 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/T9JoQxrtVy2JcxvP6) Why do adversaries sometimes cooperate to restrain their military competition? Why do they design arms control agreements with intrusive verification in some cases but rely on minimal transparency in others? Amidst ongoing international competition, arms control remains rare despite potential mutual benefits, and agreements vary dramatically in their approaches to monitoring. Jane Vaynman will discuss her book, Enemies in Agreement: Political Volatility and the Design of Arms Control (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/politics-international-relations/international-relations-and-international-organisations/enemies-agreement-political-volatility-and-design-arms-control?format=HB&isbn=9781009486507/resources#description). The book reveals how uncertainty from domestic political changes — such as leadership transitions or social unrest — can enable arms control. It identifies two paths to agreement: during periods of uncertainty, states that previously relied on informal understandings hedge by establishing lightly-monitored agreements, while those that anticipated deception take calculated risks through agreements with intensive verification. Through comprehensive data analysis and rich case studies, Jane Vaynman challenges conventional wisdom about uncertainty in international relations while offering insights for policymakers. As states confront challenges from nuclear competition to emerging technologies, understanding when arms control becomes viable is more vital than ever. Dr. Jane Vaynman is an Assistant Professor of Strategic Studies at the School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) at Johns Hopkins University. Dr. Vaynman's work focuses on security cooperation between adversarial states, the design of arms control agreements, and the effects of technology on patterns of international cooperation and competition. From 2022-2024 she served a senior advisor in the Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence, and Stability at the U.S. Department of State. Her prior academic appointments include the Department of Political Science at Temple University and the Elliott School of International Affairs, George Washington University. She was also previously a Lightning Scholar at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania, a Stanton Nuclear Security Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a Fulbright Fellow at the Carnegie Moscow Center. Dr. Vaynman received her Ph.D. in political science from Harvard University and B.A. from in international relations from Stanford University.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Experiments in Art and Geography
events.description: In this lecture, Trevor Paglen presents a framework for thinking about what happens when artistic practice and geographic method are fused together. Drawing on his work on mass surveillance, computer vision and AI, psyops, and neuroscience, Paglen will discuss art-making not simply as a means of representing geographic research, but as a geographic research method in its own right. Artistic practice can function as a form of fieldwork: a way of investigating landscapes, infrastructures, technologies, and institutions while developing new forms through which to understand them. Paglen will explore how this hybrid practice creates opportunities for collaboration across disciplines and produces forms of knowledge that do not fit neatly within conventional academic or artistic categories. The talk argues that occupying a position neither fully within art nor geography can generate questions, methods, objects, and ways of seeing that neither discipline could produce on its own. Trevor Paglen is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice explores technology, infrastructure, and perception across exhibitions, publications, and public projects worldwide. A MacArthur Fellow and 2026 LG Guggenheim Award winner, he holds advanced degrees from UC Berkeley and the Art Institute of Chicago.

events.title: California Spotlight: Wealth & Poverty
events.description: REGISTER California is one of the wealthiest states in the country, yet it also faces persistent poverty, stark economic inequality, and some of the highest costs of living in the nation. These tensions raise fundamental questions about who benefits from California's economic growth and why so many residents struggle to achieve economic security. This panel brings together leading scholars to examine the forces shaping wealth and poverty across the state. Drawing on research spanning inequality, affordability, economic mobility, and social policy, the discussion will explore the roots of California's economic divides, how they are reproduced across generations, and what is at stake for families, communities, and the future of the state. This panel will feature David Grusky, Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, and Professor of Sociology at Stanford; Marianne Page, Professor of Economics and Director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis; and Samuel Trachtman, Senior Researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative at UC Berkeley. Evan White, Executive Director of the California Policy Lab at UC Berkeley, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Goldman School of Public Policy, the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment, the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative, and the Opportunity Lab.PanelistsDavid Grusky (https://grusky.people.stanford.edu/) is Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, Professor of Sociology, Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Faculty Fellow at the Center for Population Health Sciences, Faculty Director of the Stanford Center on Poverty and Inequality, and coeditor of Pathways Magazine. He is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, a corecipient of the 2004 Max Weber Award, the founder of the Cornell University Center for the Study of Inequality, and a former Presidential Young Investigator. His recent books are Inequality in the 21st Century (with Jasmine Hill, 2017), Social Stratification (with Kate Weisshaar, 2014), Occupy the Future (with Douglas McAdam, Robert Reich, and Debra Satz, 2012), The New Gilded Age (with Tamar Kricheli-Katz, 2011), and The Great Recession (with Bruce Western and Chris Wimer, 2011).Marianne Page (https://mepage.faculty.ucdavis.edu/) is a Professor of Economics (https://economics.ucdavis.edu/) and a founding director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis (http://poverty.ucdavis.edu/). She is a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and member of the Institute for Labor Economics. She currently serves as a Co-Editor of the Journal of Human Resources, and recently completed a term serving on Governor Newsom's Council of Economic Advisors. She is an expert on policies promoting intergenerational mobility and equality of opportunity for children in the United States. Her research has appeared in economics journals including the Quarterly Journal of Economics, the American Economic Review. and the Journal of Labor Economics, and has been funded by the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.Sam Trachtman (https://besi.berkeley.edu/people/samuel-trachtman/) is a senior researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), where he leads the research program on the political economy of California. Sam completed his Ph.D. in political science in 2021 at UC Berkeley, where he honed skills in quantitative methods and policy-engaged empirical research. He has published widely in academic journals including American Political Science Review, Climatic Change, Governance, Legislative Studies Quarterly, Nature Energy, Public Opinion Quarterly, and Perspectives on Politics.Evan White (https://capolicylab.org/staff/evan-white/) co-founded the California Policy Lab, which generates research insights for government impact. Through hands-on partnerships with government, CPL performs research across issue silos and builds the data infrastructure necessary to improve programs that millions of Californians rely on. Since 2017, CPL has helped conduct 300+ projects with 75+ agency partners. As Executive Director, Evan leads the Lab's Berkeley site and authors reports on household finance, migration, and poverty. Prior to joining CPL, Evan served as Senior Advisor to the first Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Evan also served as Director of Fair Housing for northern California's largest fair housing nonprofit. He holds a joint degree in Law and Public Policy from UC Berkeley.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | What Humans Want: Models of Preference and Reward in Minds and Machines
events.description: AI alignment rests on a simple model of human decision-making: people are noisily rational agents maximizing fixed rewards that exist in the environment. This talk examines that model from both sides: minds and machines. In humans, choices follow resource-rational heuristics rather than optimal policies, and pursuing even an arbitrarily assigned goal devalues the alternatives. In machines, reward models trained on human preferences show striking biases, many inherited from pretraining rather than from the preferences themselves. Finally, LLMs share humans' inability to "un-know" biasing information, but, unlike humans, can converse with a blind, counterfactual self, substantially mitigating demographic bias and sycophancy. Brian Christian is a Research Fellow at UC Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI, where his work spans AI alignment and computational cognitive science. His research has appeared in venues like ICLR, FAccT, COLM, and PNAS and been covered by Nature and The New York Times. He is the bestselling author of three books, including Algorithms to Live By (with Tom Griffiths) and The Alignment Problem, which won the Excellence in Science Communication Award from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. He has lectured at Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta, and advised policymakers in six countries and the UN.

events.description: Description: More than 50 years after the Clean Air Act, Americans breathe far cleaner air, yet people of color and overburdened communities still breathe more pollution than everyone else. Why does unequal air persist while overall air quality improves? Drawing on recent results from hyperlocal field measurements and model simulations, I will present evidence on key drivers of air pollution disparities. With a view towards identifying solutions, we'll explore how targeted, place-based interventions could prove decisive in providing cleaner, more equitable air for all. Bio: Joshua Apte is associate professor of Environmental Engineering and Environmental Health Sciences at University of California, Berkeley. His group uses a combination of air quality models and field measurements to understand sources, processes and impacts that affect air quality from the neighborhood to global scale. Apte earned his MS and PhD in Energy and Resources (2008, 2013) from UC Berkeley.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Elynn Chen: What Makes an RL Sample Transferable? A Statistical Theory of Transfer Q-Learning
events.description: In business, healthcare, and education, sequential decisions must often be learned for a target population with little data, while abundant data exist from related populations. Transfer learning is the natural remedy, and in regression the recipe is well understood: pool source and target samples, then correct for a low-complexity difference. This talk asks whether the same recipe works for reinforcement learning (RL), and answers: only sometimes. In a Markov decision process the regression response at each stage is not the observed reward but a Bellman target that embeds the source's future value under the source's transition. Pooling therefore introduces a bias that is absent from supervised transfer and that persists even when reward functions are identical across populations; it vanishes only at the final stage of a finite horizon. This observation leads to a precise notion of a transferable RL sample and to a re-weighted targeting procedure that restores Bellman alignment: source responses are re-targeted to the target's value function and re-weighted by a transition density ratio, cascading backward through the horizon. We establish convergence rates for the resulting transfer Q-learning estimator with deep neural network function approximation, expressed through two "knobs" of task discrepancy—the reward gap and the transition density ratio—and show exactly when source data accelerate learning over single-task rates. The same principle extends to stationary MDPs with iterative Q-learning, to online RL via one-step Bellman alignment, and to composite MDPs with transferable transition components. Experiments on synthetic environments and an ICU sepsis cohort from MIMIC-III confirm the theory. Related papers: Deep Transfer Q-Learning for Offline Non-Stationary Reinforcement Learning. J. Chai, E. Chen, J. Fan. arXiv:2501.04870. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04870 Transfer Q-Learning for Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes. E. Chen, S. Li, M. I. Jordan. Electronic Journal of Statistics, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1214/25-EJS2459 Data-Driven Knowledge Transfer in Batch Q-Learning. E. Chen, X. Chen, W. Jing. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2025.2603731 One-Step Bellman Alignment Enables Provably Efficient Transfer in Online RL. E. Chen, E. Zhang, J. Chai, Y. Yan. arXiv:2601.21924. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21924 Transition Transfer Q-Learning for Composite Markov Decision Processes. J. Chai, E. Chen, L. Yang.
