events.title: José del R. Millán: Brain-Computer Interfaces: Fostering Learning, Plasticity, and Recovery
events.description: BCI control is a skill, and every component of a BCI system must support the activity-dependent plasticity that underlies skill learning and consolidation—yet the non-stationarity of EEG signals makes it hard to give users the coherent, stable feedback this process requires. I will illustrate how BCI use itself fosters learning, plasticity, and recovery, from a brain-controlled wheelchair restoring mobility, to BCI feedback that accelerates perceptual learning of small visuomotor errors, to a motor rehabilitation protocol that produces significant and lasting recovery in chronic stroke patients. I will then present two complementary strategies for stabilizing the neural features that drive the BCI: an unsupervised, Riemannian-geometry-based algorithm that corrects for feature drift in real time and lets an expert user's control features give naïve users a head start; and a neuromodulation approach in which transcutaneous electrical spinal stimulation induces cortical inhibition that sharpens sensorimotor activation and speeds BCI skill acquisition. Together, these two orthogonal approaches—one algorithmic, one physiological—show how stabilizing the neural features underlying BCI control can strengthen learning, favor cortical reorganization, and improve outcomes for both able-bodied and clinical populations.

events.title: Magdalena Ugarte: Rethinking the Normative — Settler State Planning, Indigenous Law, and Grounded Legal Pluralism | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Planning theory widely acknowledges that planning is inherently normative. Yet Western values, ethical frameworks, and visions for the future continue to shape everyday planning practice. The deep connection between planning and Western law is crucial: it often labels planning practices that challenge Western definitions of property, public interest, land use, and decision-making authority as illegal. Territorial conflicts between settler nation-states and Indigenous peoples illustrate these tensions. Drawing on years of community-engaged research with Indigenous communities in Chile, Magdalena Ugarte explores these disputes as clashing legal orders. By centering Indigenous law and land relations, we can reimagine planning in settler colonial contexts — shifting from the domination of Western law to practices rooted in legal pluralism. About Magdalena Ugarte is an associate professor in the School of Urban and Regional Planning at Toronto Metropolitan University, where she teaches planning theory, public policy, social and community planning, and studio. Her work examines the relationship between planning, settler colonialism, and other forms of racialized dispossession, as well as how communities persistently excluded from planning plan for themselves. She is currently involved in collaborative, community-based research projects that focus on Indigenous planning in Chile and Black-centered, Black-informed planning practices in Canada. She is also leading curricular changes that seek to advance racial justice and Indigenous rights in planning education. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: Translation in the Qing Poetic Imaginary | Lecture by Nathan Vedal
events.description: This talk, introducing a forthcoming monograph (Translation, Emulation, and Manchu Literary Culture), will consider the institution of a Manchu translation program in the elite Hanlin Academy. A subset of literati at the Hanlin Academy, a training ground for officials and court scholars who passed the civil service exam at the highest level, underwent a three-year program of Manchu study culminating in a final translation exam. Knowledge of Manchu gained at the Hanlin Academy, while primarily intended for bureaucratic purposes and court scholarship, is also evident in the deployment of multilingual literary effects in Chinese poetic compositions. Within Qing literary-intellectual culture, the juxtaposition of Chinese and Manchu yielded a productive venue for literary creation and self-fashioning. Speaker Bio:Nathan Vedal is an associate professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at the University of Toronto, specializing in Chinese intellectual and cultural history. He received his undergraduate degree from the Curtis Institute of Music and his PhD in Chinese history from Harvard University. His first book, The Culture of Language in Ming China: Sound, Script, and the Redefinition of Boundaries of Knowledge (Columbia University Press, 2022), won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize from the Journal of the History of Ideas.

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. NOTE: This is an in person event ONLY and will not be livestreamed. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: The Dread Heights: Tribulation and Refuge after the Syrian Revolution
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room, 230 Anthropology and Art Practice Building
events.description: Attuned to a world of brutal sieges and mass displacement, The Dread Heights details how the Islamic tradition guides refugees, relief workers, and religious scholars since the Syrian catastrophe. Through an ethnography of religious imagination and theological argumentation, Iqbal demonstrates what is at stake beyond secular frames for migration and relief. Even as refugees become objects of humanitarian concern suspended between national orders, The Dread Heights brings another suspension into view: a form of life whose gestures are illuminated by the Quranic figure of the Heights. Iqbal's ethnography pursues an unsentimental lucidity across the search for refuge, the trials of creational existence, and the ultimately enigmatic divine decree. In the shadow of war, beyond humanitarian order, Islam offers an orientation to the devastation of the present.Basit Kareem Iqbal is Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology and Associate Member in the Department of Religious Studies at McMaster University. An anthropologist and longtime academic editor, his research explores the difficulty of the present within and across distinct traditions and forms of life. He is the author of The Dread Heights: Tribulation and Refuge after the Syrian Revolution (Fordham University Press: 2025) and the co-editor of several journal issues on tribulation (2022), the destruction of loss (2023), the in/capacitation of tradition (2026), and the un/mooring of the present (forthcoming). He serves on the editorial boards of the journals Critical Times and History of the Present. He is currently working on his second monograph, tentatively titled And From What Evil He Created: Essays in Seeking Refuge, and on a translation of Yassin al-Haj Saleh's 2021 book al-Fazi' wa tamthiluh, tentatively titled Representing the Atrocious: On the Destruction of Syria and the Ruination of Form.

events.title: Fate in My Hands: The Death Penalty in the Soviet Union
events.description: From 1954 to 1991 in the Soviet Union, nearly forty thousand citizens were executed after the death penalty was reinstated as a punishment for homicide. Fate in My Hands introduces readers to the many citizens in this period—women and men of all ages and backgrounds—who found themselves on death row and tried to escape it in the only way available to them: asking for forgiveness. Examining the letters and objects the dead left behind, Skorobogatov recovers their voices and allows them to speak anew. She offers a striking portrait of life in the Soviet Union and the citizens who dreamed of new possibilities even as they faced their tragic end. Using a corpus of never-before-accessed criminal court records, Fate in My Hands brings readers not just into the police interrogation rooms, courthouses, and cells where the condemned awaited their fates, but into the homes, workplaces, and psychiatric hospitals where families and friends alike came together to pursue an elusive, bitter justice in the wake of violent tragedy.Bio: Yana Skorobogatov is a social historian of Russia and the Soviet Union whose research focuses on the late and post-Soviet periods. Her first book, Fate in My Hands: The Death Penalty in the Soviet Union (University of Chicago Press, July 2026), a history of the death penalty and the movement to abolish it in Russia and the Soviet Union, uses the records of more than 100 death penalty cases tried during the post-Stalin period to explore changing popular perceptions of the late Soviet state from Joseph Stalin's death to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Additional research interests include political-economic history, environmental history, and the history and legacies of Russian and Soviet imperialism. She is in the early stages of writing a second book that centers on the Russian island of Sakhalin and its emergence as a major epicenter of global oil after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

Across four panels, we trace an arc from the innermost self outward: how neurotechnology and algorithmic design test the limits of cognitive liberty; how deepfakes and biometric systems unsettle the law of identity; how automated decision-making challenges due process and the right to be heard; and how courts and legislatures are struggling to define what AI fundamentally is. Attendees will hear from leading scholars, technologists, and practitioners grappling with these questions in real time, as courts issue rulings, states pass conflicting statutes, and AI companies themselves debate the moral status of the systems they build.

events.title: Book Launch: "Russia's New Imperialism"
events.description: Russia's devastating invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is a manifestation of a wider phenomenon: Russia's new, post-Soviet imperialism. This book provides a theoretically informed, critical account of Russian imperialism that is attentive to the interplay between economy and ideology, coercion and hegemony, structure and agency. While economic developments go a long way toward explaining the reemergence of Russia's imperialist impulses in the twenty-first century, a purely economic logic cannot account for the dramatic shift in Russian imperialism beginning with the annexation of Crimea and the instigation of a separatist insurgency in the Donbas. Nor can objective geopolitical developments, such as US and NATO military deployments, provide an adequate explanation for this shift. Instead, this book shows how the Kremlin's reaction to the Maidan revolution was rooted in the ideological consolidation of the previous years: the emergence of a total ideology that designates the West as Russia's eternal enemy and Ukraine as the West's geopolitical pawn. Ilya Budraitskis and Ilya Matveev examine Russian foreign policy and the Kremlin's project to remake the Russian people to better serve its imperialist agenda.

events.title: Gerardo Aldana | Sak Tahn Waax, Astronomy, and Psychedelics in the History of Mayan Oracular Science
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.location: Latinx Research Center, 2547 Channing Way, Berkeley
events.description: Event Description Science is often thought of as a European development. The Mayan civilization had thousands of years of astronomical and scientific developments marginalized by colonial expansion in the early modern period. Well before the Spanish invasion, Mayan and Mesoamerican cultures were developing sophisticated scientific, medical, calendrical and mathematical frameworks that have yet to be integrated into the discussion of what constitutes advanced scientific thinking. Through the history of Mayan astronomy, we can capture dimensions of these non-European scientific developments, native to the Americas, that deserve to be revitalized and historically understood in their own cultural context.Part of the CLACS Historically Situating Mayan Scientific Knowledge event series, supported by CLACS. Co-sponsored by the Center for Science, Technology, Medicine, and Society; the Latinx Research Center; Chicanx Latinx Studies; the Department of Anthropology, the Department of History; and the Department of Astronomy. Speaker Gerardo Aldana is a Professor of Chicana and Chicano Studies at UC Santa Barbara and a historian of science specializing in Maya astronomy, hieroglyphic history, and Indigenous intellectual traditions. Trained in both mechanical engineering and the history of science, Aldana earned his Ph.D. from Harvard University and brings interdisciplinary approaches from history, archaeology, astronomy, and science studies to the study of Mesoamerica and Maya astronomy. His 2022 book, Calculating Brilliance: An Intellectual History of Mayan Astronomy at Chich'en Itza, reframes Maya astronomy as a sophisticated Indigenous intellectual tradition by reanalyzing one of the few surviving Maya texts, the Dresden Codex, which articulates robust astronomical and mathematical knowledge.

events.title: Matthew Parker (Informal BBS Seminar): Adaptive evolution of Orc1's disordered region rewires chromatin recognition and origin specification in metazoans
events.description: Sites of DNA replication initiation are specified by binding of the origin recognition complex (ORC, composed of Orc1–6) to particular chromosomal loci, but how metazoan ORC selects these sites remains poorly understood. I will discuss our work defining the mechanisms by which ORC engages chromatin in human cells and Drosophila, focusing on an Orc1 intrinsically disordered region (IDR) that mediates genomic site selection. Extending these studies across metazoans, we find that an Orc1 IDR is universally retained but has evolved under positive selection, producing distinct sequence architectures with functional consequences for DNA-binding specificity and sites of replication initiation.This seminar is partially sponsored by NIHDivision(s): Division of Biochemistry, Biophysics and Structural Biology

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSemi-artificial Photosynthesis using Formate Dehydrogenase Semi-artificial photosynthesis interfaces biological catalysts with synthetic light absorbers to overcome the inherent limitations of both artificial and natural photosynthesis. Furthermore, this emerging approach can also unlock novel reaction pathways and chemistries with significant technological potential and thus provides new opportunities that are currently not available in solar fuels or algae research. This presentation will summarise our progress in integrating the redox enzyme formate dehydrogenase into bespoke hierarchical 3D electrode scaffolds, photoelectrodes and semiconductor powders. Specifically, formate dehydrogenase immobilised on electrodes enables catalytic CO₂ reduction to formate with electrochemical reversibility and can thus operate at very low overpotential with high selectivity. The design principles for the integration of formate dehydrogenase in bespoke synthetic 3D electrode scaffolds and a detailed analysis of the biocatalyst-material interface will be presented. The understanding of the biotic-abiotic interface ultimately allows for the rational wiring of the biocatalyst into photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for the solar synthesis of fuels and chemicals. Overall, the lecture aims to demonstrate that formate dehydrogenase should be considered as unique model electrocatalyst for CO₂-to-formate conversion in solar catalysis as it enables performance currently not achievable by synthetic catalysts. A recent review on this topic is available: Liu et al., Chem. Rev., 2026, 126, 8034–8088 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.6c00095).

events.description: Bryant Walker Smith, Associate Professor of Law and (by courtesy) Engineering at University of South Carolina, will present Toward Trustworthy (Automated Driving) Companies at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Oct. 16, 2026 at 3 pm. Join us for cookie hour in the ITS Library at 2:30 p.m. Bio: Bryant Walker Smith is an associate professor in the School of Law and (by courtesy) the College of Engineering and Computing at the University of South Carolina, as well as an affiliate scholar (https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/bws) at the Center for Internet and Society at Stanford Law School. In 2025, he was a visiting professor (https://newlypossible.org/files/presentations/2025-06-28_FutureHumanitySpeech_BryantWalkerSmith.pdf) at Renmin University of China. Trained as a lawyer and an engineer, Smith advises cities, states, countries, and the United Nations on artificial intelligence, automated driving, and other emerging technologies. He has testified before the US Senate Commerce Committee (https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/blog/2026/02/opening-statement-of-professor-bryant-walker-smith-for-the-u-s-senate-commerce-committees-hearing-on-automated-driving-february-4-2026-2/), vice-chaired the US Department of Transportation's Transforming Transportation Advisory Committee (https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2025-01/TTAC%202024%20Report.pdf), served as an expert witness (https://www.plainsite.org/dockets/download.html?id=361671590&z=0992d8f5) for the State of California, coauthored the globally influential levels of driving automation (https://www.sae.org/standards/j3016_202104-taxonomy-definitions-terms-related-driving-automation-systems-road-motor-vehicles), drafted a ULC model law (https://www.uniformlaws.org/committees/community-home?CommunityKey=4e70cf8e-a3f4-4c55-9d27-fb3e2ab241d6) for automated driving, and (in 2012) taught the first legal course dedicated to automated driving. Smith's article on "The Trustworthy Company" is forthcoming in the Georgetown Law Journal, and his article on "Regulating Robotaxis" is forthcoming in the Southern California Law Review. His publications are available at newlypossible.org (http://newlypossible.org/). Before joining the University of South Carolina, Smith led the legal aspects of automated driving program at Stanford University, clerked for the Hon. Evan J. Wallach at the United States Court of International Trade, and worked as a fellow at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. He holds both an LL.M. in International Legal Studies and a J.D. (cum laude) from New York University School of Law and a B.S. in Civil Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. Prior to his legal career, Smith worked as a transportation engineer.

Schulte Strathaus served on the selection committee of the Berlinale Forum and was the Founding Director of the Berlinale section Forum Expanded. events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Castrato Phantoms Book Chat w/ Martha Feldman (University of Chicago)
events.description: Castrato PhantomsBook ChatMartha Feldman (University of Chicago) Held in the Townsend Center's Geballe RoomMartha Feldman (Ferdinand Schevill Distinguished Service Professor, Music & Theater and Performance Studies, University of Chicago) discusses her sweeping account of the castrato dilemma in its end stages as an index of modern consciousness. How can we write the histories of a complex multigenerational past when it is mired in obfuscations that stretch from the most intimate of family events to the doings of the Roman church to the machinery of the Italian state? This was the challenge Feldman faced when she crossed paths with descendants of the last castrato to star in Roman chapels, whose uncle turned out to be the iconic film director Federico Fellini. Some years after their first encounter, she offers a book that unravels the entanglements of family traumas with the secret suppressions of the Vatican and fascist state. Her Castrato Phantoms: Moreschi, Fellini, and the Sacred Vernacular in Rome (Zone Books, 2026) provides compelling answers that follow up on her Berkeley Bloch Lectures (published as The Castrato: Reflections on Natures and Kinds, University of California Press, 2015). Her novel concept of the sacred vernacular makes sense of the profanations of everyday sacred rituals and objects, traced here through sound recordings, literary texts, photographs, films, and letters. Drawing on Roman archives, a previously unknown family archive, and a wealth of Roman historical documentation, she deploys the sacred vernacular to rewrite the history of old-world hauntings in a modern key. Feldman will deliver a half-hour lecture before conversing with Prof. James Q. Davies. A Q & A with the audience will follow. Prof. Ramona Naddaff will moderate.

events.title: Film Screening: Raging Bull
events.description: Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro make the biography of boxer Jake LaMotta into a visceral meditation on existential suffering. Eschewing the romance associated with the sport, Raging Bull shows the struggle of an athlete whose willful determination to succeed on his own terms takes its toll on all those around him—friends and adversaries in equal measure—before he is undermined by self-loathing. Every punch is framed, lit, and cut for maximum impact, with black-and-white cinematography inspired by James Wong Howe. "A fusion of Hollywood genre with personal vision . . . closer to poetry than pulp. Its sculptural weight can only be appreciated on the big screen" (Amy Taubin, Village Voice).

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Language & Literacy across the Disciplines
events.description: Language and literacy are embedded in every subject students encounter. This Saturday Seminar is an opportunity for TK-12 educators from across the Bay Area to strengthen language and literacy practices in their classrooms. Saturday Seminars are led by UC Berkeley's content area experts, who represent California Subject Matter Project sites and partner organizations in the field of education. Workshops are teacher-centered professional learning spaces that emphasize practical tools, approaches, and strategies to bring to classrooms on Monday! Session 1 Workshops 9:15 - 10:45 AMScience and Literacy: Speaking, Writing & Reading to Learn Science (k-5) We often think of literacy and science as academic opposites. But we can't do science without reading, writing, listening, and communicating. This workshop will focus participants on two questions: In what ways can learning science develop students' language skills? and, How do language skills support sense-making in science? Teachers will engage in a shared learning experience using a classroom science activity, and engage in a debrief discussion, examining interconnections of science and literacy. This workshop is most applicable for elementary school teachers, but all are welcome! Sarah Pedemonte currently serves as Director of the Bay Area Science Project. She has worked at the Lawrence Hall of Science for over 20 years, designing curriculum and facilitating professional learning for K-12 teachers in science.Place-Based Literacy: Exploring Local Infrastructures to Understand Global Topics (6-12) Our infrastructures reveal our connections to the broader world, our local social relations and political structures, our histories, our values, and more. This workshop introduces the concept of infrastructures and models lessons through which students can actively engage with the infrastructures that affect their own lives. Participants will also be introduced to a set of teacher-produced lessons for middle and high school students. Materials are drawn from a year-long program supported by California Global Education Project and ORIAS. Shane Carter is the Program Coordinator for ORIAS (the Office of Resources for International and Area Studies) at the University of California, Berkeley and a host-site director for California Global Education Project. In both roles Shane introduces educators to a range of international topics and provides them with tools to help students develop global competence. Shane is a former high school history-social studies teacher and the creator of two podcasts: Points In Between and Future Imperfect.Elizabeth Aracic has taught English and Social Studies for over 23 years at Miramonte High School in Orinda. She has taught 14 courses and was also librarian, and is always open to sharing curriculum (and never minds if you adapt it and make it your own). Suzy Anderson has taught seventh grade World History and English for 25 years at Mill Valley Middle School, and for the last few years has taught the Global Studies elective, focusing on sustainable development. Engaging Language Learners from the Start: Comprehensible Input and Guided Practice (TK-12) In this workshop, teachers will experience a short, comprehensible input story about choosing the ingredients for a salad. They will participate in guided practice activities to process the new material, practicing communicative language and literacy strategies to engage students. Nancy Salsig is Co-Director of the Berkeley World Language Project at UC Berkeley. She taught high school French and Spanish for 36 years. Currently she supervises student teachers at CSU East Bay and St. Mary's College.Who's in the Lead? Building Student Criticality about AI with the 4D Framework (6-12) AI literacy requires more than knowing how to use a tool. It requires students to question when AI should be used, how it works, whose experiences shape it, and how its decisions affect people. In this interactive workshop, participants will apply the 4D Framework, Determination, Data, Design, and Deployment, to realistic classroom scenarios across the grade spans. Participants will collaborate to identify bias, examine tradeoffs, and consider where human judgment must remain in the lead. Participants will leave with a practical questioning routine and adaptable prompts that help students evaluate AI critically, ethically, and equitably while preserving productive struggle and learner agency. This workshop is designed for 5th to 12th grade teachers, instructional coaches, and teacher leaders across content areas. All are welcome. Vanessa Lujan, Ph.D. is Director of K-12 STEM Education at the Lawrence Hall of Science. Vanessa brings deep expertise in K-12 STEM systems change, equity-centered leadership, and professional learning that helps districts bridge from vision to classroom practice. Her work focuses on building district capacity for STEM education while advancing learning environments where all students can see themselves as capable STEM thinkers and problem solvers.Eric Greenwald, Ph.D., Learning Sciences Researcher at the Lawrence Hall of Science, leads projects that advance research, learning design, and systems change at the intersection of science, math, computational thinking, and AI. In particular, he studies how learning can be designed toward a more robust and equitable socio-technical understanding of AI systems that better positions learners for criticality and agency in a world we are increasingly living together with AI.Crystal Menzies, Ph.D., Equity Research & Learning Systems Lead at the Lawrence Hall of Science, brings a scholar-practitioner perspective rooted in asset-based research, curriculum design, and professional learning to the AI K-12 Network team Session 2 Workshops 11:00 AM - 12:30 PMUsing Visual Historical Evidence to Support Analytical Thinking (6-12) This workshop focuses on using visual sources to analyze historical narratives with middle and high school History-Social Science students. Teachers will discuss a theoretical framework used for analyzing evidence, and the classroom inquiries this framework can inspire. Teachers will leave with at least 2 concrete strategies for analyzing images and realia that connect to structured academic conversation as well as focused content readings. Jason Muñiz is Director of the UC Berkeley History-Social Science Project. During his time with the project he has led the development of UCBHSSP's programmatic support for implementing Ethnic Studies by leading professional development for administrators and educators, developing interdisciplinary History-Social Science curriculum, and spearheading an initiative to bring UC Berkeley's Ethnic Studies and History institutional resources to High School teachers.Building Language, Ideas, and Sense of Self through Writing (6-12) Writing is a powerful medium for exploring ideas in all disciplines, making connections, and building language. In this workshop, participants will write for themselves, explore ways to embed writing across disciplines, and analyze multilingual students' writing for what it reveals about language practice. This workshop is best suited for secondary teachers, but all are welcome! Hillary Walker is Director of the Bay Area Writing Project (BAWP), which focuses on strengthening writing instruction in classrooms by sharing the expertise of writing teachers. She is a veteran secondary writing teacher, and also teaches community college courses in African American Studies, Ethnic Studies, and History.Metacognition: Making Meaning of Language by Making Thinking Visible (TK-12) So much of literacy is about making our thinking visible, identifying what our brains are doing as we encounter language, text, media, and the world around us. Metacognition is a deeply transferable skill that invites all learners to pause, to uncover what is normally invisible (even to ourselves), and thus to understand when/how we are accessing information and making meaning, and when/how we are getting stuck. Participants will connect with their personal metacognitive/reflective practices, explore and experience several research-based metacognitive strategies, and complete a mini-design sprint to incorporate a strategy into an upcoming lesson/unit/project. This session is applicable to TK-12 teachers and leaders, all are welcome! Abby Benedetto, College & Career Alliance Support Network (CCASN), has taken on designing and changing systems for the last two decades from a wide variety of roles and perspectives. Abby is able to draw upon her lived experience of the decade she spent as a classroom teacher and leader, a decade of working shoulder to shoulder with educators in this country and abroad, as well as a unique ability to help educators make connections between what they know and their aspirational vision for where they want to go. Abby is proud to serve as one of CCASN's lead collaborative partners.Dr. Tameka L. McGlawn, Executive Director and Principal Investigator, College & Career Alliance Support Network (CCASN), is a fourth-generation educator, scholar, counselor, and servant leader with more than 30 years of experience advancing educational equity through research, practice, policy, and systems leadership. She partners with district systems, networks, institutions, and organizations to strengthen leadership capacity and support sustainable and measurable transformation. She helps education leaders translate research into practical strategies that strengthen equity, coherence, and continuous improvement.Scaffolding Authentic Resources for All Learners (TK-12) Explore strategies to scaffold authentic resources to engage students. Learn how to make real-world texts accessible and meaningful to learners at all levels. The workshop centers on culturally responsive strategies across cultures. Nancy Salsig is Co-Director of the Berkeley World Language Project at UC Berkeley. She taught high school French and Spanish for 36 years. Currently she supervises student teachers at CSU East Bay and St. Mary's College.

events.title: La maison des bois: Episodes 1–3
events.description: Epic yet intimate, sweeping yet personal, La maison des bois stands as one of the greatest achievements in the history of television, as well as legendary director Maurice Pialat's magnum opus. Commissioned for Télévision Française in 1971, this seven-episode, nearly four-hundred-minute miniseries considers the impact of World War I on a simple French family living in the countryside. Applying a naturalistic focus to their subject, Pialat and screenwriter René Wheeler capture both the historical scope of the conflict and the subtle ways that a small town's quotidian routines and rituals—church, school, tavern—are indelibly touched by it.

events.title: Kamila Shamsie | The Mahomedali Habib Distinguished Lecture on Pakistan
events.description: The Institute and Pakistan@Berkeley (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/berkeley-pakistan-initiative), a campaign to broaden and deepen Pakistan related research, teaching and programming at UC Berkeley, are proud to announce the eleventh "Mahomedali Habib Distinguished Lecture on Pakistan (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/mahomedali-habib-lecture-series)" by the award winning writer and novelist, Kamila Shamsie (https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/697055/best-of-friends-by-kamila-shamsie/). Join us as the acclaimed Pakistani writer talks about her craft, and journey, and her latest novel, Best of Friends, with Harsha Ram (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/harsha-ram), Associate Professor in the Departments of Comparative Literature and of Slavic Languages and Literatures, UC Berkeley. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Institute's FB page: ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) _________________Author Bio Kamila Shamsie is the author of eight novels, which have been translated into over 30 languages, including Burnt Shadows and A God in Every Stone. Her previous novel Home Fire won the Women's Prize for Fiction, was long listed for the Man Booker Prize and shortlisted for the Australian Book Industry Award for International Book. A Vice-President and Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature and Professor of Creative Writing at the University of Manchester, she was one of Granta's 'Best of Young British Novelists' in 2013. She grew up in Karachi, and now lives in London. Her new novel is Best of Friends, published in September 2022. _________________ Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) The event is FREE and OPEN to the public.

events.title: Film Screening: White Nights
events.description: This adaptation of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's tale about displaced, disconnected people drifting along crossing, doubling paths was shot in moody black-and-white on a soundstage simulacrum of Livorno, Italy. With it Luchino Visconti veered away from verisimilitude and toward an emphatically subjective style—from neorealism to neoromanticism. As a quiet man who accidentally befriends a troubled, lonely young woman (Maria Schell) and finds himself playing understudy for the absent object of her affections (Jean Marais), Marcello Mastroianni mingles subtly passionate yearnings with a characteristic note of annoyance. His character is both distrustful of and seduced by the romantic dreams that preoccupy the woman he loves.

events.title: TEDxBerkeley 2026
events.location: Pauley Ballroom; 2495 Bancroft Way Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Every experiment begins with a question: What if? Experimentation launches us on a new journey into the unknown. Every trial, whether it leads to success, failure, or something in between, becomes a part of the discovery process. Xperiment is about leaning into uncertainty with intention; trying what hasn't been tried, breaking patterns, and embracing curiosity without the promise of a clear outcome. Just as a lab experiment requires curiosity, design and iteration, so do the choices we make in our lives, communities, and fields of work. Sometimes we follow a precise method; other times we stumble into accidental breakthroughs. At times our results can confirm our expectations, while at others they challenge us to rethink everything. But regardless of the result, each trial moves us closer to new ways of thinking or being. At TEDxBerkeley 2026: Xperiment, we invite you to challenge assumptions, explore unfamiliar ideas, and embrace the uncertainty that comes with trying something new. From bold discoveries to unexpected turns, Xperiment is about the curiosity that pushes us beyond what we already know. Join us on October 18th, 2026 at Pauley Ballroom as we ask new questions, test new possibilities, and see where they take us. Check out our speaker lineup at www.tedxberkeley.org.

events.title: Film Screening: Shaihu Umar
events.description: This important work of Nigerian cinema was long thought to be lost, but in 2016 negatives and prints of the film were found in the archive of the Nigerian Film Corporation. Arsenal Filminstitut restored the film, which was shown at the 2018 Berlinale Forum. Shaihu Umar, set in northern Nigeria at the end of the nineteenth century, is based on the eponymous novella by Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, who would later become the first prime minister of independent Nigeria. It starts with a discussion between students and their respected teacher, the Islamic scholar Shaihu Umar, who tells them about his modest background and many trials and tribulations, including slavery.

events.title: Judy Collins Sweet Judy Blue Eyes: The Farewell Tour
events.description: Sunday, October 18, 3pm Vocal CelebrationJudy CollinsSweet Judy Blue Eyes: The Farewell Tour Program: A living legend of American music, Judy Collins returns to Berkeley with a retrospective concert that looks back on her six-decade-long career and pays tribute to the generations of artists she has influenced. A contemporary of Bob Dylan and Joan Baez, the folksinger, songwriter, and activist became a household name with hit renditions of Joni Mitchell's "Both Sides Now" and Stephen Sondheim's "Send In the Clowns." She has recorded 55 albums and, as a testament to her impact on the music world, artists such as Rufus Wainwright, Shawn Colvin, Dolly Parton, and Leonard Cohen honored her legacy with the album Born to the Breed: A Tribute to Judy Collins. "A lovely trip down memory lane, allowing Collins, an ever-engaging raconteur, to weave together songs with stories and remembrances from across her legendary career"—Toronto Guardian

events.description: In a review for the Village Voice, J. Hoberman called The King of Comedy the "richest, most intelligent Hollywood movie of 1983. . . . Between them, [Martin] Scorsese, Robert De Niro and screenwriter Paul Zimmerman have created an American archetype: Rupert Pupkin . . . the celebrity-crazed would-be standup comedian who attaches himself to TV talk-show host Jerry Lewis. . . . The King of Comedy is a meditation on American celebrity but—dealing as it does with rampant aggression, pure megalomania, visceral embarrassment and pathetic humiliation—it's a good deal more disturbing." Sandra Bernhard makes an indelible appearance as Pupkin's partner in obsession.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

Bringing together the volume's editors and contributors, the panel will consider the enduring significance of Akhtaruzzaman Elias's landmark novel Khwabnama, exploring its distinctive engagement with history, memory, politics, and rural life in Bengal and its place in Bengali and global literary thought.Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies and Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley.PanelistsEditor: Firdous Azim (https://www.bracu.ac.bd/about/people/firdous-azim-phd?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of English and Humanities at BRAC UniversityEditor: Naveeda Khan (https://anthropology.jhu.edu/directory/naveeda-khan/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of Anthropology at Johns Hopkins UniversityNasrin Khandoker (https://juniv.edu/teachers/nasrin.khandoker?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Postdoctoral Fellow, University College CorkDina M. Siddiqi (https://liberalstudies.nyu.edu/about/faculty-listing/dina-siddiqi.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Clinical Professor in Liberal Studies at New York UniversityKamran Ali (https://experts.utexas.edu/kamran_ali?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of Anthropology at the University of Texas at AustinHumayun Kabir (https://qc-undergraduate.catalog.cuny.edu/departments/PSCI-QC/faculty?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Adjunct Assistant Professor of Political Science at Queens College, CUNYNaeem Mohaiemen (https://arts.columbia.edu/profiles/naeem-mohaiemen?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Associate Professor of Visual Arts at Columbia University. _________________DATE: Mon, Oct 19, 2026 TIME: 9 am Berkeley | Calculate your local time (https://www.thetimezoneconverter.com/)ZOOM: Register HERE (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_h0uy7TJ1TZGt45ZkYO4k_w) _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter)_________________ ABOUT THE BOOKDreams' Navel (https://uplbooks.com/shop/9789845067119-dreams-navel-23890?utm_source=chatgpt.com) provides an interdisciplinary exploration of Akhtaruzzaman Elias's Khwabnama, a monumental work of Bengali modernist fiction. This collection of essays examines how the novel enriches official nationalist histories of Bangladesh and the 1947 Partition. By attending to the 'minutiae of locality'—the marshes, myths, and memories of rural North Bengal —contributors from anthropology, literature, and political science demonstrate Elias's unique ability to weave the oneiric and the magical into historical experience. The volume offers fresh reflections on subaltern agency, gendered domesticity, and the evocative sensory world of the Bengali rural landscape. Dreams' Navel provides a transformative vantage on a classic text, positioning Elias not just within the Bengali canon, but as a vital and provocative voice in global conceptual inquiry. This scholarly tribute is essential for readers seeking to understand the enduring power of Elias's literary imagination and its resonance in the postcolonial world. She is a founding member of Naripokkho, a women's activist group in Bangladesh.Naveeda Khan is Professor of Anthropology at Johns Hopkins University, where she is affiliated with Women, Gender, Sexuality; Islamic Studies; Environmental Science and Studies; and the Department of Comparative Thought and Literature. Her publications include In Quest of a Shared Planet: Negotiating Climate from the Global South (2023), River Life and the Upspring of Nature (2022), and Muslim Becoming: Aspiration and Skepticism in Pakistan (2012). events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: The single-genaerator problem for $C^*$-algebras
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Chun Guang Li, Northeast Normal UniversityThe single-generator problem asks whether every simple separable $C^*$-algebra can be generated by a single element. It is closely related to the classical generator problem for von Neumann algebras. In this talk, I will first review the background and some of the main developments concerning this problem. I will then present recent joint work on several classes of $C^*$-algebras. we prove that each Villadsen algebra of the first type is singly generated. In contrast, we construct a Villadsen algebra of the second kind that is not singly generated. For crossed products, we prove that if σ is a minimal homeomorphism of a compact metrizable space $X$, then $C(X)times Z$ is singly generated. Finally, we establish that the reduced group $C^*$-algebra $C_r^*(F_2)$ of the free group on two generators is singly generated. The results presented in this talk arise from joint work, in different collaborations with George A. Elliott, Zhuang Niu and M. Ruzicka.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of changes in risk appetite around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite, consistent with the literature on the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Most of the variation in asset prices and risk appetite is unexplained by conventional interest-rate surprises, which points to an important role of risk appetite in monetary transmission. Proxy SVARs with two separately-instrumented monetary policy shocks—a risk-free rate shock and a risk appetite shock—show the empirical importance of this channel. Risk appetite shocks have large, significant, and theory-consistent effects on inflation, output and employment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks become insignificant or switch signs as soon as a risk-appetite shock is included in the VAR setup. Our evidence suggests that monetary transmission works primarily through risk asset prices and risk appetite. Standard estimation of monetary transmission based solely on interest-rate surprises misses most of these effects for two main reasons: First, the impact of interest-rate policy on asset prices is time-varying and state-dependent. Second, central bank communication can affect risk appetite and asset prices in ways that go beyond changes in the expected policy path.

events.title: Jürgen Dinkel | All remains in the Family: A History of Inheritance in the US and Europe Since 1800
events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: PMB Seminar with Adam Steinbrenner | Seeing like a plant: immune recognition and signaling by cell surface receptors
events.description: Plants sense extracellular cues through several hundred cell surface receptors. The most rapidly evolving group of receptors is the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (RLPs), which transduce immune signals as a bipartite receptor complex with the adapter SOBIR1. In recent years many new examples of immunogenic patterns detected by specific RLPs have been described, highlighting their versatility as immune sensing modules. I will discuss unique features of the RLP family that mediate recognition and signaling functions. For recognition, RLPs encode an extracellular island domain, which allosterically couples ligand binding to co-receptor recruitment. For signaling, RLPs lack a kinase domain typical of most receptors, but the short cytoplasmic tail domain can encode signaling through different defense pathways. For both recognition and signaling functions, I will describe new insights from our study of Inceptin Receptor (INR), which detects caterpillar-derived peptide elicitors and evolved 28 mya in a single subtribe of legumes. Since both island and tail domains are small (~10-60 aa) shared features of all RLPs, they may represent modular, editable handles to engineer plant immune systems.

events.title: Moving Ideas into Action in a Shifting Policy Landscape: A Symposium Marking Twenty Years of the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment
events.organizer: Center for Law, Energy & the Environment
events.description: Join Berkeley Law’s Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) for a symposium marking the research center’s 20th anniversary. Berkeley Law established the Center for Law, Energy, and the Environment (CLEE) in 2006 – a time when California was launching bold, world-leading policies to address climate and environmental issues. At the same time, the federal government was walking back from its commitments and trying to limit the State’s authority. Fast forward twenty years and the policy landscape looks similar, albeit much more dire – both in the urgency of the climate crisis and the scale of federal rollbacks and attacks on state action. Over the past twenty years, CLEE has honed its focus and expertise in this shifting and dynamic policy landscape. A large portion of CLEE’s work has focused at the subnational level and has resulted in significant contributions from the local to global scale. This half-day symposium, marking the 20th anniversary of CLEE, welcomes new and long-time friends and partners of CLEE to discuss the challenges, impacts, and significance of environmental law and policy scholarship and how to make a difference in a dynamic policy landscape. Speakers include: Senator Henry Stern ‘09 (CA District 27) Professor Dan Farber, Founding Faculty Director of CLEE Rick Frank, Founding Executive Director of CLEE Rachel Morello-Frosch, Inaugural Associate Provost of Energy, Climate, and the Environment, UC Berkeley The symposium will be held from 2:00–5:00 p.m., and followed by a reception with drinks and hors d’oeuvres. We are grateful to our event sponsors, Brownstein, Nossaman, Orrick, Sheppard, The Tomblin Family Foundation, Willis Towers Watson, and Wilson Sonsini. We encourage you to RSVP at your earliest convenience due to limited space. Please email Maia Baltzley at maia.baltzley@berkeley.edu within 7 days of the symposium if you will need an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.), or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History
events.description: Salt lakes are some of the world's most extraordinary ecosystems, but nearly all of them―from the Great Salt Lake to the Aral Sea��are drying up, a harbinger of dust storms, rising sea levels, and worsening human health. Caroline Tracey's book Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History, a hybrid work of memoir and geographic research, spans the American West, Mexico, Argentina, Kazakhstan and beyond, documenting salt lakes, their loss, and the efforts underway to save them, as well as Tracey's relationships to the lakes. In this talk she will describe the making of the book, including how it draws on her training in geographic methods and on additional creative sources such as Mormon diaries, Soviet realist novels, Australian Aboriginal paintings, and techniques of memoir and the personal essay. Caroline Tracey is the author of Salt Lakes: An Unnatural History (W.W. Norton, 2026). After receiving her PhD in Geography from the University of California, Berkeley, she became an independent writer and journalist specializing in the Southwestern US, Mexico, and their borderlands. Her work has appeared in numerous publications and has received a Fulbright fellowship, the Waterston Prize for Desert Writing, an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writer's Grant, and a Creative Capital State of the Arts Award.

events.title: Descriptive Set Theory Working Seminar: Failure of the $L^1$ pointwise ergodic theorem
events.description: Speaker: MohammedSaid Alhalimi, UC BerkeleyThe goal of this talk is to explore some concrete examples of the failure of the ergodic theorem. I will review the work of Nevo and Stein which establishes pointwise ergodic theorems of $F_2$ actions for $L^p$ functions ($p1$) using spherical averaging operators. Following Tao (2015), I will introduce an example of a measure-preserving system with an $L^1$ function whose sequence of averages is unbounded thereby witnessing the failure of $L^1$ pointwise ergodic theorems for $F_2$ actions.

events.organizer: Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice
events.description: The criminal legal system we confront today is the product of nearly 1000 years of development during which new institutions, new powers, and new myths about crime and punishment have been installed in response to periodic crises originating in the political and economic conflicts of society. The result is a kind of carceral leviathan that can appear in many ways to suit the needs of the time and overcome moral and practical criticisms. In the lecture, Professor Simon will review this history and how it continues to be relevant today to those seeking to reform or even abolish it. Jonathan Simon graduated from Berkeley law with a JD and a PhD in the Jurisprudence and Social Policy program. Simon is the author of three books and many articles on the criminal legal system in the United States and its relationship to shifts in American society and democracy. He has been a professor at Berkeley Law since 2003. Lunch will be served inside of Room 170 starting at 12:50 PM. RSVPs will be prioritized.

events.title: Indispensable but Invisible: Legal Expertise and Juridical Capital in the Governance of Late Imperial China | Lecture by Li Chen
events.description: During the Qing period (1644–1912), late imperial China was in theory governed by approximately two thousand local administrators who were appointed for their mastery of the Confucian classics rather than for their administrative or legal expertise. How did these scholar-officials actually carry out the daily tasks of local governance, including judicial administration? Based on a forthcoming monograph, this talk analyzes the training and roles of the thousands of legal specialists who advised local officials behind the scenes and handled most of the judicial and other substantive administrative work on their behalf. Despite their important functions in local governance, these legal specialists were ideologically marginalized. This talk, as well as the larger study from which it is drawn, provides new insights into why they became so indispensable to Qing law and governance and why they remained obscure to outsiders and modern researchers. Speaker BioLi Chen, J.D. (UIUC) and Ph.D. (Columbia), is Professor of History at the University of Toronto, with a cross-appointment at the Faculty of Law. Among his extensive publications on the intersection of law, culture, and politics in Chinese and international history since the 1500s is his monograph,Chinese Law in Imperial Eyes: Sovereignty, Justice, and Transcultural Politics(Columbia University Press, 2016), which received the 2018 Joseph Levenson Book Prize from the Association for Asian Studies and an Honorable Mention for the 2017 Peter Gonville Stein Book Award from the American Society for Legal History. He has recently completed another monograph,Invisible Power in China: Legal Expertise, Statecraft Traditions, and Cultural Politics, 1651–1911. He was the founding president (2014–2017) of the International Society for Chinese Law and History and currently serves on the boards of that organization and the American Society for Legal History. He also serves on the editorial boards ofLaw and History Review,Law & Social Inquiry, and theJournal of World History. He is currently working on book projects on the Qing system of Autumn Assizes for major criminal cases and on the remarkable but little-known history of Qing legal lineages.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra seminar: Traces on Weak Lorentz Ideals and Nonclassical Weyl Laws
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote online talk
events.description: Speaker: Raphael Ponge, University of OttawaIn Connes' noncommutative geometry, traces on operator ideals play the role of the integral. The basic examples are Dixmier traces and, more generally, positive normalized traces on the weak trace class $L_{1,\infty }$. This setting is taylored to classical Weyl laws, where eigenvalues decay like $j^{-1/p}$. Many natural operators, however, obey nonclassical Weyl laws with logarithmic corrections, $\lambda _j\sim c, j^{-1/p}(\log j)^q$. Examoles include Dirichlet Laplacians on infinite-volume domains, Dirac operators on open manifolds with cusps and assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, the Dirac operator of Connes–Moscovici whose eigenvalues are the imaginary parts of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Such operators lie outside$L_{1,\infty }$, in weak Lorentz ideals associated with regularly varying functions. This talk is about traces on these ideals. I will first show that an asymptotic additivity property for eigenvalue partial sums allows us to define Dixmier traces directly in terms of eigenvalue sequences. This leads to a spectral characterization of operators on which all Dixmier traces agree, answeing a question of Connes in this setting. I will then go beyond Dixmier traces and consider the whole class of positive normalized traces. The main tool is an extension of Pietsch's correspondence which relates traces on weak Lorentz ideals to invariant functionals on sequence spaces and places Dixmier traces within a broader picture. It yields a spectral characterization of operators on which all postive normalized traces agree. This extends results of Pietsch and Semenov–Sukochev–Usachev–Zanin for$L_{1,\infty }$. Combined with an extension of the Birman–Solomyak perturbation theory, it shows that operators satisfying Weyl laws take the same value on all positive normalized traces. I will also discuss a further notion, hypermeasurability. Finally, I will illustrate these results with examples, including the Riemann Hypothesis, the logarithm of th Laplacian, and products of Laplacians. This is joint work with Yongqiang Tian (Central South Univesity, Changsha, China).

events.title: (Julia Mahamid) Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: "In-cell structural biology at a systems level"
events.description: Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: (https://thevalleefoundation.org/programs/kdl) Recent technological breakthroughs in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) open the disruptive possibility to image macromolecular complexes in their native cellular or multicellular context at close to atomic resolution, and can directly reveal how their different conformational states and interaction networks are linked to biological functions. We advance sample preparation techniques for in-cell cryo-ET, including cryo-focused ion beam thinning and 3D correlative (super resolution) fluorescence microscopy. Preparations of such site-specific 'electron-transparent windows' enable the assignment of macromolecular structures directly from the high-resolution three-dimensional stills captured by cryo-ET when aided by an array of methods, including computational patter recognition and novel developments of genetically-encoded molecular tags. Furthermore, integration of multiple data sources is key to the interpretation of the mined structural signatures. For example, using the genome-reduced human pathogen Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a minimal cell model, we established the synergistic application of whole-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry and cellular cryo-ET to determine an in-cell integrative structural model of actively transcribing RNA polymerases coupled to translating ribosomes. Our contributions to computational methods now allow resolving these molecular machines to high resolution, reveal small molecule antibiotics bound to their active site in ribosomes within the intact pathogen, provide snapshots of their structural dynamics, and illuminate functions of previously unknown macromolecular complexes. Such integration of cutting-edge methods unlocks an enormous potential for mechanistic understanding at a system-spanning level by in-cell structural biology.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with David Henkin
events.description: In Out of the Ballpark (Oxford, 2026), David Henkin (History) reconsiders the character, meaning, and delights of baseball by exploring the game's unusual features and the sport's many resonances with other aspects of modern life. To this end, he abandons several assumptions and mythologies that underlie most approaches to histories of baseball: that it is unique among sports and fundamentally different from other kinds of entertainment; that it is specific to the United States; that it has changed fundamentally in recent years; and that the keys to understanding it lie primarily in examining what happens on the field of play. Instead, Henkin moves across time and space to examine baseball's history since the nineteenth century and beyond US borders. He takes readers inside the structures of clubs and leagues, interprets the sacred scripture of rulebooks, and illuminates some of baseball's rites and rituals that are often associated with honor and manhood. He charts baseball's significance along the routes of American and Japanese imperial expansion and the shifting maps of race and ethnicity in the US. Baseball is found at negotiating tables that pit capital against labor and in pivotal moments in the history of mass media. He shows us how baseball might offer a complex and capacious space for thinking about such things as spectatorship, success, community, order, and contingency in the modern world. Henkin is joined by Alva Noë (Philosophy). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - All that is compute transforms into concrete: Monopoly rent and the fixity of AI's infrastructure
events.description: In the capitalist imaginary, artificial intelligence is narrated on dematerialization. In this telling, capital has escaped the weight of human labor via the frictionless circulation of data. This paper argues the opposite: the AI economy is a geography of fixity, where training large language models requires warehouse-scale data centers anchored to specific territories by the demands of energy, infrastructure, and available land. Two analytical categories theorize this fixity. The first concerns the monopoly control of location and network proximity: value is extracted from whoever sits closest to the data, controls the interconnection, and commands the lowest latency. The second concerns the monopoly control of computation itself: training frontier AI models is capital-intensive, technically scarce, and concentrated in a handful of firms who can extract a tribute that is not reducible to productivity but to infra/structural position. Both forms of extraction are rent. And both are responses to a profitability crisis in the AI sector driven by rising fixed capital requirements that outpace returns. We draw on financial filings, industry reports, and field observations in Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley to show that what appears as an agglomeration economy is better understood as rent extracted through the strategic fixity of capital in digital infrastructure. Dillon Mahmoudi (dillonm@umbc.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography and Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland Baltimore County. and Alan Wiig (alanwiig@ufl.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography at the University of Florida. They recently published a book chapter, Land for AI: Data Center Real Estate Markets in The Inner World of Artificial Intelligence (2026).

events.title: Matrix on Point: The State of U.S. Immigration Enforcement and Surveillance
events.description: REGISTER Federal immigration enforcement in the United States is increasingly shaped by the convergence of surveillance technologies, data systems, and on-the-ground policing practices. From AI-assisted identification tools to information-sharing across agencies, these developments are transforming how enforcement operates, and raising urgent questions about civil liberties and democratic oversight. This panel will bring together scholars to examine the social and political consequences, and the stakes for rights in an era of technological governance. The panel will feature David Hausman, Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley Law School, Caitlin Patler, Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and Jennifer Urban, Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law School. Deirdre Mulligan, Professor in the UC Berkeley School of Information, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Asian American Research Center, the Center for Race and Gender, the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative, the Goldman School of Public Policy, and the UC Berkeley School of Information.Matrix On Point (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/matrix-on-point/) is a discussion series promoting focused, cross-disciplinary conversations on today's most pressing issues. Offering opportunities for scholarly exchange and interaction, each Matrix On Point features the perspectives of leading scholars and specialists from different disciplines, followed by an open conversation. These thought-provoking events are free and open to the public. Panelists David Hausman (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/david-hausman/#tab_profile) is an Assistant Professor at Berkeley Law School. He does empirical work on U.S. immigration enforcement, mostly using government data disclosed in response to Freedom of Information Act requests. He also co-directs the Deportation Data Project (https://deportationdata.org/). Before joining Berkeley, he practiced law at the ACLU Immigrants' Rights Project in New York City.Caitlin Patler (https://gspp.berkeley.edu/research-and-impact/faculty/caitlin-patler) is Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and faculty affiliate of the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative (BIMI), Berkeley Population Center, and the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment. Dr. Patler's research examines US immigration and criminal laws, legal statuses, and law enforcement institutions as drivers of socioeconomic and health disparities.Jennifer M. Urban (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/jennifer-urban/#tab_profile) is a Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law, where she is Director of Policy Initiatives at the Samuelson Law, Technology & Public Policy Clinic (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/experiential/clinics/samuelson-law-technology-public-policy-clinic/). Her research focuses on information policy: intellectual property, privacy and data protection, and security. She regularly collaborates with technologists and academics in disciplines other than law to develop empirically grounded understandings of how new technologies and the regulatory structures around them interact with civil liberties, innovation, and creative expression. In March 2021, Urban was appointed by California Governor Gavin Newsom to be the inaugural Chair of the California Privacy Protection Agency Board.Deirdre K. Mulligan (https://www.ischool.berkeley.edu/people/deirdre-mulligan) (moderator) is a Professor in the School of Information at UC Berkeley, a faculty Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/bclt/), and a co-organizer of the Algorithmic Fairness & Opacity Working Group (http://afog.berkeley.edu/). Mulligan's research explores legal and technical means of protecting values such as privacy, freedom of expression, and fairness in socio-technical systems. Her book Privacy on the Ground: Driving Corporate Behavior in the United States and Europe (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/privacy-ground), a study of privacy practices in large corporations in five countries, with UC Berkeley Law Prof. Kenneth Bamberger was published in 2015 by MIT Press. Mulligan served as Principal Deputy U.S. Chief Technology Officer at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, (https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/) and Director of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office (NAIIO), in the Biden-Harris Administration. In November 2025, Mulligan was appointed to Governor Newsom's California Innovation Council. REGISTER
